cues.text: On June 2, 1668, the Saturday within the octave of Corpus Christi, Father Nicolas Nezan, pastor of the small church of Les Ulmes in France, exposed the Blessed Sacrament.
He did so for public adoration and began incensing the monstrance as the faithful sang the hymn Pange Lingua.
A Figure in Place of the Host
As the singing reached the verse 'Verbum caro panem verum' — 'the Word made flesh, true bread' — those present reported that the Host itself seemed to give way to a man's shape.
The figure had light-brown hair falling to his shoulders, a luminous face, hands crossed over one another, and a white tunic covering him entirely.
The apparition lasted, by the accounts of those present, for roughly a quarter of an hour, witnessed not by one or two individuals but by the whole congregation gathered for the adoration.
Word of the event reached Bishop Henry Arnauld within days, and he ordered a formal inquiry into what the parish had seen.
After examining the testimony, the bishop authorized devotion to the event.
The associated Host remained enshrined in a specially built recess in the church for more than 130 years.
That recess is still visible in the church today.
During the French Revolution, fearing the Host would be profaned by revolutionary violence, the vicar of nearby Puy-Notre-Dame consumed it himself rather than risk its desecration.
The parish of Les Ulmes kept the anniversary of the apparition as a solemn annual observance well into the following centuries.

The event received renewed scholarly attention at the International Eucharistic Congress of Angers in 1901 and again at the National Eucharistic Congress of 1933, where a full session studied the 1668 account.

An old print depicting the vision, along with the empty recess that once held the Host itself, remain the parish's lasting physical connection to an event witnessed, by every surviving account, by an entire congregation at once.
